slides.title: How many of each kind of test
points: The testing pyramid says: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, a few end-to-end tests at the top.
It balances confidence, speed and maintenance.

slides.title: Three layers
points: Unit tests check small pieces of logic in isolation, in milliseconds.
Integration tests check that pieces work together: code with a real database, two services over an API.
End-to-end tests drive the whole system like a user; they catch the most and break the most.
Each bug found is best pinned at the lowest layer that can catch it.

slides.title: Shapes that go wrong
points: An 'ice-cream cone' (mostly end-to-end, few unit tests) is slow and flaky.
Only unit tests can pass while the parts don't fit together.
Some teams prefer a 'trophy' with more integration tests; the point is a deliberate mix.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Unit and integration tests on every commit; end-to-end on merge or nightly.
Test run times watched like product performance.
Each production bug gets a test at the right layer.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Choosing which cases to test
points: You can't test every input. Test design picks the few cases most likely to find bugs.
A handful of well-chosen cases beats hundreds of random ones.

slides.title: Partitions, boundaries, combinations
points: Equivalence partitioning: group inputs that should behave the same, and test one from each group.
Boundary values: bugs cluster at edges, so test just below, at and just above each limit.
Decision tables and state transitions cover rules and workflows systematically.
Pairwise testing covers combinations of options without testing every one.

slides.title: Coverage against effort
points: Too few cases miss bugs; too many slow the suite and hide intent.
Code coverage shows what ran, not whether the checks were meaningful.
Negative cases (invalid input, failures) are often forgotten.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Test cases written from requirements before the code is done.
Edge cases listed explicitly in tickets.
Reviews of tests, not just code.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Making a bug easy to fix
points: A good bug report lets someone else reproduce the problem quickly and understand why it matters.
Vague reports get bounced back or ignored.

slides.title: Steps, expected, actual, impact
points: A clear title naming the symptom and where it happens.
Exact steps to reproduce, from a known starting state.
Expected result versus actual result, with screenshots, logs or a recording.
Environment (version, browser, device, account type) and impact (who's affected, how badly).

slides.title: Detail against time
points: Minimising the steps takes effort and saves developers far more.
Severity (how bad) and priority (how soon) are different; say both.
One bug per report, so each can be tracked and closed.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A bug template in the tracker.
Intermittent bugs reported with how often they happen and what was tried.
Retesting after the fix, then closing.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Tests that run themselves
points: Automation frameworks drive applications through code: browsers (Playwright, Cypress, Selenium), APIs, mobile apps.
They turn repeated manual checks into fast, repeatable ones.

slides.title: Stable, readable, maintainable
points: Locate elements by role, label or test id, not by fragile CSS paths.
Wait for conditions (an element visible, a request done), never fixed sleeps.
Page objects or helpers keep tests readable and changes in one place.
API tests check logic faster and more reliably than UI tests where possible.

slides.title: Automation isn't free
points: Every automated test needs maintenance as the product changes.
Automating unstable features wastes effort.
Some checks (look and feel, exploratory) still need people.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Tests in the same repository as the code, reviewed with it.
Runs in CI with screenshots and traces on failure.
A rule for what gets automated and what stays manual.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Each test starts from a known state
points: Tests that share data or depend on order fail unpredictably.
Isolation means each test sets up what it needs and leaves nothing behind.

slides.title: Create, use, clean up
points: Create test data in the test (factories, fixtures) rather than relying on whatever's in a shared database.
Use unique names or ids so parallel tests don't collide.
Reset state between tests: transactions rolled back, containers recreated, or data deleted.
Never use real customer data; generate synthetic data.

slides.title: Speed against independence
points: Fresh data for every test is slower; sharing read-only reference data is often fine.
Mocks make tests fast and can drift from the real dependency.
Production-like data finds more bugs but brings privacy risk.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Database containers per test run (Testcontainers).
Seeded, synthetic datasets for staging.
Tests that pass in any order and in parallel.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Checks a change must pass to merge
points: Quality gates in CI stop changes that break tests, lower coverage on new code, add vulnerabilities or fail linting.
They make quality automatic instead of a final phase.

slides.title: Fast, meaningful, enforced
points: Required checks on every pull request: build, unit and integration tests, linters, security scans.
Gate on new code (coverage of changed lines), not on legacy totals.
Keep the required set fast; run slow suites on merge or nightly.
A failed gate blocks the merge; bypassing needs a recorded reason.

slides.title: Strict against productive
points: Too many slow gates push people to batch changes or bypass.
Flaky gates teach people to rerun until green; fix flakiness quickly.
Metrics like coverage can be gamed; review the tests too.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Branch protection rules with required checks.
Dashboards of pipeline time and failure causes.
Ownership for each gate.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Tests that fail without a real bug
points: A flaky test passes and fails on the same code.
Flakiness erodes trust: people stop believing red builds, and real bugs slip through.

slides.title: Common causes
points: Timing: fixed sleeps, race conditions, animations, slow responses.
Shared state and order dependence between tests.
External dependencies: real networks, third-party services, time and dates.
Randomness without a fixed seed.

slides.title: Retry or fix
points: Automatic retries hide flakiness and real intermittent bugs alike.
Quarantining keeps the build green while the test is fixed, but must be temporary.
Sometimes the flakiness is a real product race condition worth fixing.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Flaky-test reports from CI history.
Clock and network faked in tests.
An owner and a deadline for each quarantined test.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Checking services agree, without running them all
points: Contract tests check that a provider (an API) still gives what each consumer expects.
They catch breaking changes between services earlier and faster than full end-to-end tests.

slides.title: Consumer-driven contracts
points: Each consumer records the requests it makes and the responses it relies on (a contract).
The provider's CI replays those contracts against its own code.
A change that breaks a consumer's contract fails the provider's build.
Tools like Pact manage contracts and versions.

slides.title: Narrow but fast
points: Contracts check shape and key behaviour, not whole business flows.
Keeping contracts up to date takes discipline from both teams.
They don't replace a few end-to-end tests of critical journeys.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A contract broker showing which versions are compatible.
Deploys blocked when a contract isn't verified.
Schema checks (OpenAPI) as a lighter alternative.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Will it hold up under load?
points: Performance tests measure response times and capacity under realistic and extreme load.
They find bottlenecks before users do.

slides.title: Load, stress, soak
points: Load test: expected traffic, checking latency percentiles against targets.
Stress test: beyond expected, to find the breaking point and how it fails.
Soak test: steady load for hours, finding memory leaks and slow degradation.
Use production-like data volumes; small data hides slow queries.

slides.title: Realism costs effort
points: Unrealistic scripts (one endpoint hammered) give misleading results.
Testing shared environments disturbs other teams.
Averages hide the slow tail; report p95 and p99.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: k6, Gatling, Locust or JMeter scripts in version control.
Performance budgets checked before big releases.
Results compared with the previous run to catch regressions.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Checking the product works for everyone
points: Accessibility testing checks that people using keyboards, screen readers, magnification or voice can use the product.
It combines automated checks with manual testing.

slides.title: Automated plus manual
points: Automated tools (axe, Lighthouse) catch missing labels, low contrast and invalid ARIA, about a third of issues.
Keyboard testing: every action reachable with Tab, Enter and Space, with visible focus.
Screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, NVDA): content announced sensibly, in order.
Zoom to 200 % and large text sizes without breaking layouts.

slides.title: Early is cheap
points: Fixing accessibility late means rework; test components as they're built.
Passing automated checks doesn't mean usable.
Testing with disabled users finds what experts miss.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: axe checks in component and end-to-end tests.
An accessibility checklist in the definition of done.
Issues ranked by WCAG level and impact.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: A team's suite is 400 end-to-end browser tests that take 90 minutes and often fail randomly. What change helps most?
choices: Move most checks down to unit and integration tests, keeping a few end-to-end tests for critical journeys
why: Lower layers are faster and steadier; keep the top thin.

newQuestions.stem: A field accepts ages 18 to 65 inclusive. Which set of test values is strongest?
why: Boundaries and just beyond are where off-by-one bugs live.
Misses the upper limit and invalid values.

newQuestions.stem: Which bug report is most likely to get fixed quickly?
choices: 'Checkout: Pay button does nothing on Safari 17 (macOS). Steps: … Expected: payment page. Actual: no response; console error attached. Affects all Safari users.'
'Payments don't work sometimes, please fix ASAP'
why: It's reproducible, specific and shows impact.

newQuestions.stem: UI tests break every time designers change CSS classes. What's the more robust way to find elements?
choices: Use roles, accessible labels or dedicated test ids instead of styling selectors
why: These reflect meaning and stay stable when styles change.

newQuestions.stem: Tests pass when run one by one but fail when run in parallel. What's the most likely cause?
choices: Tests share data or state (same user, same record); give each test its own data
The CI machine is too slow
why: Shared state makes results depend on timing and order.

newQuestions.stem: Developers routinely click 're-run' until a flaky CI check turns green. What's the right response?
choices: Quarantine and fix the flaky tests, and track flakiness so the gate stays trustworthy
why: A gate is only useful if failures mean something.

newQuestions.stem: A test checks a 'created today' label and fails every night just after midnight UTC. What's the cause and fix?
choices: It depends on the real clock and time zone; control the clock in the test (inject or fake the date)
The server is slow at night
why: Tests that read the real clock change behaviour by time of day.

newQuestions.stem: A backend team renames a response field and two frontend apps break in production. How would contract testing have helped?
choices: The consumers' contracts would fail in the backend's CI before the change merged
It would rename the field automatically
It would make the apps faster
why: The provider learns it breaks a consumer before shipping.
This is exactly what it catches.

newQuestions.stem: A load test against a database with 1,000 rows shows great response times. Production has 10 million rows. What's the concern?
choices: Queries that are fast on tiny data can be slow at production size; test with production-like volumes
None; the code is the same
Load tests should use no data
why: Data size changes query plans and timings.

newQuestions.stem: Automated accessibility checks report zero issues. Is the page accessible?
choices: Not necessarily: automated tools catch only some issues; test with a keyboard and a screen reader too
why: Much of accessibility needs human judgement.
